title: Gazpacho
subtitle: The cold Andalusian soup that turns raw summer vegetables into something silky and bright
excerpt: A blended cold Spanish soup made from ripe tomatoes, red pepper, garlic and olive oil, finished with a drizzle of your best oil.
sourceNotes: Traditional Andalusian cold soup, a staple of southern Spanish summer cooking.

recipe.batchNotes: Keeps refrigerated for up to 3 days. The flavour improves overnight.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make at least an hour ahead and chill thoroughly. Overnight is better.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cold Spanish soup made from raw blended vegetables, typically served in summer.

content.text: This gazpacho serves 4 and takes 15 minutes of hands-on work plus at least 1 hour of chilling time. It is entirely uncooked, so the quality of the tomatoes makes or breaks the result. Use the ripest, most flavourful tomatoes you can find.

Blend in stages: blitz the vegetables first until completely smooth, then stream in the olive oil while blending. The breadcrumbs act as an emulsifier and give the soup its characteristic body and slight creaminess. Do not skip them. Season generously and taste again after chilling, as cold dulls salt.
Soak the breadcrumbs in 3 tablespoons of water for 5 minutes to soften.
Put the tomatoes, red pepper, garlic and soaked breadcrumbs into a blender. Blend on high for 2 minutes until completely smooth.
With the blender running on medium, slowly stream in the olive oil. The soup should look slightly lighter in colour and have a silky, emulsified texture.
Add the lemon juice and season well with black pepper. Blend briefly to combine.
Pass through a fine sieve if you want a very smooth, restaurant-style finish, or leave as-is for a more textured result. Both are valid.
Transfer to a large jug or bowl, cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour. Taste again for seasoning once chilled. Serve in cold bowls with a drizzle of olive oil.

items.problem: The gazpacho tastes flat and bland
items.solution: Cold dulls seasoning. Always taste again after chilling and add more salt and lemon juice as needed.

items.problem: The texture is watery rather than silky
items.solution: Either the breadcrumbs were skipped or the olive oil was not streamed in slowly enough to emulsify. Blend for longer with a fresh piece of bread added.

items.problem: The soup has separated in the fridge
items.solution: Whisk or blend briefly before serving. A little separation is normal; it does not mean the soup has spoiled.

content.text: is from Andalusia in southern Spain, where summer temperatures make a cold meal non-negotiable. It was originally a peasant dish made by pounding stale bread with vegetables and oil in a pestle and mortar. Blenders have replaced the mortar, but the principle is unchanged. It is served in restaurants as a starter and drunk cold from a glass at home. Make it the day before for the best flavour.
